subject: HelixBio private deployment — VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN

Subject: Re: HelixBio private deployment — initial ask

Thanks Kim — quick summary of our constraints so you have context before the call: 

- Data must remain in our EU tenancy (no egress for PII).
- We have strict network zoning: multiple on-prem networks with overlapping RFC1918 ranges (10.0.0.0/8 used broadly).
- Our infra team prefers minimal peering due to cross-account exposure policies.
- We can accept a managed interface endpoint model if it doesn’t require VPN uptime ops from our side.

Can you outline pros/cons of VPC Peering vs PrivateLink (interface endpoints) vs site-to-site VPN? Latency is important (sub-50ms targets for inference), but compliance and surface-area control are higher priority.

Cheers,
Alex
HelixBio — Head of Platform

Alex — thanks for the context. Looping in Karthik (SE) and Connor (Solutions) to ground the tradeoffs. High level below; Karthik will follow with a short matrix and a latency/cost ballpark.

Short take: 
- VPC Peering: simplest for flat L3 connectivity and low latency, but requires non-overlapping IPs and broad network trust across accounts. Not great if HelixBio is uncomfortable granting peering across many internal subnets.
- PrivateLink / Interface Endpoint: exposes specific services via ENIs (AWS) or equivalent. Great for least-privilege exposure, works when IP ranges overlap, and reduces blast radius. Slightly higher per-request cost and introduces an extra network hop but typically preserves low latency for regional traffic.
- Site-to-Site VPN (IPSec): works with overlapping ranges via NAT, fully customer-managed or co-managed. Good if customer wants to avoid cloud cross-account trust. Operational burden and higher tail latency; also less friendly for autoscaling cross-account control planes.

Attachments: I posted a quick matrix (access-patterns-matrix.xlsx) and the network diagram you sent into the Jira/Confluence link for the deal.

Next step: Karthik, can you propose a recommended pattern and an ops checklist (NAT, route table changes, firewall rules, monitor/SLA) for Helix?

Thanks,
Kim

Subject: Re: HelixBio private deployment — technical tradeoff matrix

Team / Alex — I sketched a short decision matrix and a recommended pattern for HelixBio below. Quick note: these are cloud-agnostic concepts but call out AWS terms where helpful.

Decision matrix (summary):
- Non-overlapping IP & trust required: VPC Peering — pros: L3 flatness, best latency, no extra per-request charges. cons: cannot peer across accounts with overlapping IPs, broad exposure, harder firewall segmentation.
- Overlapping IPs or least-privilege exposure: PrivateLink — pros: service-level exposure, works with overlapping ranges, minimal route table changes, smaller blast radius. cons: interface endpoints have ENIs in the customer VPC (security review), per-GB and endpoint-hour cost potentially higher, slight added hop.
- On-prem or strict control: S2S VPN — pros: minimal cloud trust, supports NAT to resolve overlaps, well-understood by netops. cons: higher latency variance, maintenance windows, manual failover complexity, not ideal for high QPS inference without dedicated circuits.

Recommended for HelixBio (given constraints: EU tenancy, overlapping on-prem ranges, strict zoning): PrivateLink-first with a fallback encrypted S2S VPN for legacy on-prem hosts. Rationale: PrivateLink gives us a narrow, auditable ingress surface (interface endpoints per service), works even when Helix has overlapping RFC1918 ranges, and limits the need for broad peering agreements. For very latency-sensitive clusters that can be readdressed into a non-overlapping space, VPC Peering is still the lowest-latency option — we can propose a phased approach.

Operational checklist (high level):
- Helix: create interface endpoints for the Redwood service (we provide the endpoint service name).
- Helix: open outbound HTTPS (443) to our endpoint ENIs and restrict by SGs to only app subnets.
- Redwood: publish a service name (com.redwood-inference.helix-prod) and provide interface endpoint SPN + failover region plan.
- NAT considerations: where on-prem overlaps exist, we recommend NAT on prem or a small re-addressing window for subnets doing inference traffic.
- Monitoring & SLA: implement endpoint-level health checks + route failover to our dedicated region. Provide logging (Flow logs + endpoint logs) for audits.

I'll attach a quick cost/latency estimate and a sample implementation snippet for AWS PrivateLink.

-Karthik
Staff Solutions Engineer

Thanks Karthik — this is helpful. A few clarifying questions from our infra/security: 

1) If we go PrivateLink, will the endpoint ENIs be in our account and thus visible in our inventory? (We need them in inventory for compliance scanning.)
2) For interface endpoints, what's the expected additional p99 latency hit (our target is <50ms end-to-end for inference requests inside the region)?
3) If we later ask Redwood to fail traffic to a dedicated peered VPC (non-overlapping) for ultra-low latency, how disruptive is that migration?

Also: we prefer to avoid wholesale readdressing of on-prem subnets; NAT is acceptable for a limited set of IP ranges. Can you include NAT guidance in the checklist?

From: connor_obrien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>

Date: Wed, 2 Jul 2025 15:04:00 -0700
Subject: Re: HelixBio private deployment — next steps and ops plan

Nina — answers inline and next steps.

1) Endpoint inventory: Yes. Interface endpoint ENIs are created in your VPC and are visible like any other ENI. They show up in inventory/CMDB and can be scanned by your tooling (we recommend tagging and a short naming convention).

2) Latency: PrivateLink typically adds a single internal hop. In our benchmarks in the eu-west-1 region, typical additional p50/p95 was ~2–6ms, p99 ~8–14ms depending on instance types and path. That said, the end-to-end p99 for inference depends on model latency + network. For most customers we meet the <50ms target with PrivateLink; for turbo-low-latency use cases we recommend a peered VPC with colocated inference cluster. We can provide a small perf test during the POC.

3) Migration to peering: If you later readdress or carve a non-overlapping subnet for inference, switching to VPC Peering is straightforward from a routing standpoint (create peering, update route tables, remove interface endpoints). Plan for a short maintenance window to adjust DNS (if you use private DNS names) and to flip source/destination checks. We can automate a blue/green cutover to reduce disruption.

NAT guidance (high level):
- Keep NAT translation scopes small — only NAT subnets/reserved CIDRs that will talk to Redwood.
- Use SNAT with deterministic mapping where possible for firewall auditability.
- Document NAT mappings in your CMDB and automate rotation/purge.

Next steps:
- Kim/Marissa: confirm commercial OK to include interface-endpoint support in the Dedicated/Private quote.
- Alex/Nina: if agreeable, we’ll schedule a 2-hour POC: 1) create interface endpoint + security review, 2) run perf tests with a sample model, 3) validate logs/audit delivery.

I’ll drop a short runbook and the POA into the Jira link.
